Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON, England (CNN) -- Nothing says true love like releasing a caged butterfly, don't you think? Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin are to be paid $5 million for the picture rights to their wedding. The butterflies are reported to be the piece-de-resistance of England's most anticipated celebrity wedding of the year. Wayne Rooney, the best English footballer of his generation, and Coleen McLoughlin, his High School sweetheart, were to marry in an estimated $10 million ceremony in Italy Thursday. As they kiss, guests are apparently meant to open boxes and release the butterflies. The moment has been pilloried widely in the British media, tacky and over the top they all think, but is it just sour grapes? It has been a long and, at times, bumpy road for the couple to the altar. One littered with fierce criticism from the British press, which has enjoyed nothing more than lampooning Rooney and McLoughlin for being 'common.' The Daily Mail once even asked: "Is this Britain's ghastliest couple?" Rooney has been dubbed "Shrek" and "Mr Potato Head" due to his looks and his background as the son of a school dinner lady who grew up on a council estate is often referred to in a disparaging way. McLoughlin, meanwhile, has been subjected to page upon page of bitter stories about her weight, shopping sprees and her lack of closeness to Victoria Beckham. There has also been fierce criticism over the fact she has managed to become a millionaire in her own right. It's all down to Rooney apparently, and nothing to do with her appearing to be quite a decent person, who did well at school and has cleverly managed to parlay some of her fame into various media and advertising projects. Anyone who has seen her television show -- Coleen's Real Women -- can see she is a decent, bubbly person, who is very good at putting people at ease. Much to the media's fury, the couple have sold the rights to cover the wedding to OK magazine for a record $5 million. However they're not pocketing all the cash themselves, with an undisclosed sum from the fee to be donated to the Claire House children's hospice in Cheshire -- where McLoughlin's disabled foster sister Rosie is cared for. The queen's grandson, Peter Phillips and his bride Autumn Kelly, recently received $1m from Hello magazine to cover their wedding but they didn't receive an eighth of the opprobrium now directed at the more generous, but lower class, Rooney and McLoughlin. Moreover, in lieu of presents, Rooney and McLoughlin have also asked guests to donate money to the Alder Hey children's hospital in Liverpool. The wedding might be over the top, with a private yacht and luxury jet for guests (they are covering the guests' costs), expensive plonk and a $200,000 wedding dress, but at least the couple have worked hard for what they have. Their success despite a working-class background appears to be the greatest source of frustration for critics. It's just not on that someone who wasn't born into privilege and didn't go to a posh school can enjoy their wealth. That would be ugly. If anything, the couple's relationship and success is a triumph over adversity. They have known each other since McLoughlin was 12, but she spent two years fending off Rooney's entreaties to go out on a date. He finally got his chance when he saw her struggling to fix a broken bicycle chain. He rode over to help, popped the question again and got a yes. Surely they should be congratulated for creating their own modern fairytale complete with butterflies? The opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of the writer.

outputs.L2:
LONDON, England (CNN) — What could symbolize romance more clearly than butterflies being set free from boxes?

Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin are reportedly receiving $5 million for exclusive photographs of their wedding, and the butterfly release is expected to be the showpiece of England’s most eagerly awaited celebrity marriage of the year.

Rooney, regarded as the finest English footballer of his generation, was due to marry McLoughlin, his high school sweetheart, in Italy on Thursday. The ceremony was estimated to cost $10 million. According to reports, guests would open containers and release butterflies as the couple kissed.

British newspapers have widely ridiculed the idea as gaudy and excessive. But could that criticism simply reflect resentment?

The couple’s journey to marriage has been lengthy and occasionally difficult, marked by relentless attacks from a British press that has taken particular pleasure in mocking Rooney and McLoughlin as “common.” At one point, the Daily Mail even posed the question: “Is this Britain’s ghastliest couple?”

Because of his appearance, Rooney has been labeled “Shrek” and “Mr Potato Head.” His upbringing is also frequently mentioned with contempt: he is the son of a school dinner lady and was raised on a council estate.

McLoughlin has endured endless hostile coverage about her weight, expensive shopping trips and supposed failure to form a close friendship with Victoria Beckham. Critics have also attacked the fact that she has become a millionaire independently.

The suggestion is that she owes everything to Rooney, rather than to her own qualities. Yet she appears to be a genuinely pleasant person who succeeded at school and has skillfully turned some of her celebrity into opportunities in advertising and the media. Viewers of her television program, *Coleen’s Real Women*, can see that she is cheerful, likable and particularly good at making others feel comfortable.

To the apparent outrage of the press, the couple sold coverage rights for their wedding to *OK* magazine for a record $5 million. They will not, however, keep the entire amount. An unspecified portion is to be donated to Claire House children’s hospice in Cheshire, where McLoughlin’s disabled foster sister, Rosie, receives care.

Peter Phillips, the queen’s grandson, and his wife, Autumn Kelly, recently accepted $1 million from *Hello* magazine for access to their wedding. Yet they faced nowhere near one-eighth of the condemnation now aimed at Rooney and McLoughlin, who are both more generous and from a less privileged social background.

The couple have also asked their guests to make donations to Liverpool’s Alder Hey children’s hospital instead of buying wedding presents.

Certainly, the celebrations may be extravagant. Plans reportedly include a private yacht, a luxury aircraft for attendees—with the couple paying their guests’ expenses—costly wine and a wedding gown worth $200,000. Even so, Rooney and McLoughlin have worked hard to achieve what they possess.

What appears to trouble their detractors most is that they have succeeded despite coming from working-class families. To some critics, it seems unacceptable for people who were neither born into privilege nor educated at elite schools to enjoy their money. That attitude is what is truly unattractive.

If anything, both their relationship and their achievements represent victory in the face of hardship. They have known one another since McLoughlin was 12, although she resisted Rooney’s requests for a date for two years. His opportunity finally arrived when he noticed her having difficulty repairing a bicycle chain. He cycled over, helped her, asked her out once more—and this time she agreed.

Shouldn’t they be praised for building their own contemporary fairy tale, butterflies included?

The views stated in this commentary belong exclusively to its author.

Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin’s wedding in Italy was one of the most lavish British celebrity events of its era. The celebrations reportedly stretched over several days and included luxury yachts, designer clothes, elaborate receptions, and the release of butterflies after the ceremony. The couple also sold exclusive coverage of the event to a magazine in a deal said to be worth a record $5 million. Given Rooney’s status as a leading footballer and McLoughlin’s prominence as a celebrity and fashion figure in her own right, intense public interest was inevitable.

Yet much of the British media’s coverage went beyond reporting the scale and cost of the occasion. Newspapers and commentators mocked the couple’s choices as gaudy, excessive, or lacking in taste. Particular attention was paid to the theatrical details of the wedding, while their accents, Liverpool backgrounds, clothing, and spending habits were treated as evidence that wealth had not given them social refinement. The implication was often that the couple had entered a world of luxury to which they did not naturally belong.

This response exposed a familiar form of class prejudice. Extravagance among aristocrats or members of established society is frequently presented as tradition, glamour, or eccentricity. When similar displays come from people with working-class backgrounds, however, they are more likely to be described as vulgar or embarrassing. Rooney and McLoughlin’s wedding therefore became an opportunity for commentators to police social boundaries, ridiculing not simply the event but the couple’s perceived failure to conform to elite standards of restraint and “good taste.”

The treatment of McLoughlin was especially revealing. She was often portrayed as merely a footballer’s wife, despite having developed an independent public profile and secured lucrative work in fashion, television, writing, and advertising. Her commercial success did not protect her from criticism; in some respects, it appeared to intensify it. Her confidence, spending power, and ability to profit from celebrity challenged the expectation that she should remain a passive companion to her famous husband. As a young working-class woman who had turned media attention into a career, she attracted resentment shaped by both class and gender.

The magazine agreement was also used against the couple. Selling wedding photographs was characterized as crude commercialization, even though exclusive celebrity deals had long been a standard part of the entertainment industry. The reported size of the payment made the arrangement unusually visible, but it also demonstrated the couple’s market value and their ability to control access to a major personal event. What critics framed as greed could equally be understood as a calculated business decision in a media culture already profiting from their private lives.

None of this means that the wedding was beyond criticism. Its expense and spectacle could reasonably be questioned, particularly in a society marked by economic inequality. But the tone of the coverage often suggested that the real offense was not extravagance itself. It was extravagance displayed by people whose origins, speech, and tastes marked them as working class. The ridicule directed at Rooney and McLoughlin shows how celebrity journalism can turn aesthetic judgment into social stigma, allowing old hierarchies to survive beneath the language of fashion, taste, and entertainment.

Their wedding thus became more than a celebrity spectacle. It revealed the uneasy relationship between fame, money, and class in Britain. Rooney and McLoughlin had achieved wealth and influence, but media coverage repeatedly reminded them—and the public—that success does not automatically confer social acceptance. Their treatment illustrates how tabloids can celebrate working-class celebrities as popular icons while simultaneously mocking them for failing to behave like the traditional elite.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style opinion commentary defending Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin’s lavish Italian wedding against criticism from the British media.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Rooney wedding backlash smacks of British class snobbery

*Opinion: Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin’s lavish Italian celebration may not suit everyone’s taste. But the outrage says more about Britain’s media than it does about the couple.*

The British press has long enjoyed a complicated relationship with wealth. Aristocratic extravagance is treated as tradition. Royal opulence becomes national pageantry. But when a footballer from a working-class background spends lavishly, the champagne suddenly tastes vulgar.

That double standard hangs over coverage of Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin’s Italian wedding.

Reports have lingered over the cost, the celebrity guests and the luxury surrounding the event, often with a tone somewhere between fascination and moral disapproval. Yet Rooney earned his fortune through an extraordinary talent performed under relentless public scrutiny. If he and McLoughlin chose to spend some of that money celebrating their marriage with family and friends, that is hardly a public scandal.

No taxpayer was presented with the bill. No constitutional principle was at stake. This was a private couple holding an expensive party with their own money.

Critics may reasonably find the spectacle excessive. Lavish weddings are not inherently more meaningful than modest ones, and money cannot guarantee a happy marriage. But personal taste is not a moral verdict. One person’s gaudy indulgence is another’s once-in-a-lifetime celebration.

The more uncomfortable question is why certain kinds of wealth are granted dignity while others are mocked. Britain is often more forgiving of inherited privilege than earned affluence—especially when the newly wealthy retain regional accents, popular tastes and visible enthusiasm for enjoying their success.

Rooney and McLoughlin did not emerge from a country estate or a society dynasty. Their public image has been shaped by football, fashion, tabloid attention and their Liverpool roots. Much of the criticism appears directed not simply at how much they spent, but at the supposedly “wrong” people spending it.

There is also rich hypocrisy in newspapers condemning the scale of a celebrity wedding while filling page after page with its details. The same outlets that scold stars for extravagance depend on photographs, guest lists and breathless descriptions of designer clothes to attract readers. The moral outrage is part of the product.

None of this means the couple should be immune from criticism. Public figures invite commentary, and celebrity culture often deserves skepticism. But criticism should be proportionate—and honest. A lavish wedding is not evidence of bad character. Nor does working-class success become more respectable only when it is expressed with upper-class restraint.

Rooney and McLoughlin wanted a grand Italian wedding. They could afford one. They had one.

Britain’s media need not admire their choices. But it might examine why a footballer’s extravagance provokes ridicule while the excesses of the establishment are so often romanticized.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce an article arguing that press coverage of Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin’s wedding reflects class prejudice, mentioning the butterfly release, the $5 million photo deal, and their charitable donations.
counterfactuals.output:
## The Rooney Wedding Coverage Exposed Britain’s Class Prejudice

When Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin married in Italy, much of the British press treated the event less as a wedding than as an opportunity to put a wealthy working-class couple on trial. The clothes, the location, the guests and even the entertainment were presented as evidence of vulgarity. Behind the jokes lay an old prejudice: money may allow people from modest backgrounds to enter elite spaces, but it does not guarantee that the media will consider them entitled to be there.

The coverage of the butterfly release was especially revealing. Releasing butterflies at a wedding is certainly open to criticism on environmental or animal-welfare grounds. Yet many reports seemed less interested in those questions than in turning the spectacle into a metaphor for the couple’s supposed bad taste. An extravagant gesture by an aristocrat or society heiress might have been described as eccentric, romantic or theatrical. In Rooney and McLoughlin’s case, it became another exhibit in the prosecution of “chav” excess.

The same double standard surrounded the reported $5 million photo deal. Exclusive wedding photographs are hardly an invention of footballers and their partners. Royals, actors and other celebrities have long negotiated access to major life events, often with far less moral outrage. Nevertheless, the Rooney deal was repeatedly framed as grasping and commercial, as though accepting millions from a magazine were uniquely distasteful when done by two people who had grown up outside the traditional establishment.

That framing also obscured an inconvenient part of the story: the couple’s charitable donations. They reportedly directed money connected with the celebrations toward charitable causes and encouraged generosity rather than simply treating the wedding as an exercise in personal consumption. Such giving does not place every choice beyond criticism, but it complicates the caricature of a couple concerned only with display. Too often, the donations appeared as a footnote while every conspicuous detail was promoted as front-page proof of their lack of refinement.

Class prejudice rarely announces itself openly. It operates through differences in vocabulary and tone. The rich are “lavish”; the newly rich are “flash.” Establishment figures are “colourful”; footballers are “tacky.” A grand society wedding is a pageant, while a grand footballer’s wedding is an obscenity. The amount of money involved may be similar, but the cultural permission to spend it is not.

Rooney and McLoughlin did not have to be models of restraint for the coverage to be unfair. Their wedding was undeniably extravagant, and elements such as the butterfly release deserved scrutiny. But scrutiny is not the same as sneering. By dwelling on the spectacle, treating the $5 million photo deal as evidence of moral failure and giving less prominence to their charitable donations, the press reinforced a familiar hierarchy: working-class people may become rich, but they will still be mocked for failing to perform wealth in the “right” way.

The real story was therefore larger than one celebrity wedding. It was about who is permitted glamour, who is granted eccentricity and whose extravagance is automatically recoded as vulgarity. The reaction to the Rooney wedding suggested that, in parts of the British media, class boundaries remain firmly in place—even when the people being judged can easily afford to cross them.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a lively celebrity-news column about Rooney and McLoughlin’s $10 million wedding. Contrast the mockery of their working-class backgrounds with the softer treatment given to royal weddings.
counterfactuals.output:
## When Wayne Met Coleen: Why Is a Footballer’s Fairy Tale “Vulgar” but a Royal One “Tradition”?

By celebrity-wedding standards, Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin’s reported $10 million Italian extravaganza had everything: designer clothes, private jets, luxury yachts, pop-star entertainment and enough glossy exclusivity to keep the tabloids fizzing for weeks.

It also had something the British class system finds irresistible: two working-class kids spending serious money.

The sneering arrived almost on cue. The Rooneys’ wedding was portrayed as gaudy, excessive and proof that wealth cannot buy taste. Coleen’s fashion choices were inspected as though they were evidence in a criminal trial. Wayne’s every ungainly pose became a punchline. Their roots—Croxteth, football, big families, sudden riches—were not merely biographical details; they were treated as the joke itself.

Yet when royalty stages a lavish wedding, the vocabulary changes. Extravagance becomes “pageantry.” A convoy is “ceremonial.” Jewels are “historic.” Vast security costs are “the price of national celebration.” Where a footballer’s hired yacht suggests vulgar display, a royal carriage represents continuity. One couple splashes out; the other “lifts the nation.”

Of course, Rooney and McLoughlin invited attention. A wedding reportedly costing around $10 million is hardly an exercise in modesty, and lucrative magazine arrangements blur the line between private celebration and commercial spectacle. But royal weddings are spectacles too—meticulously branded, globally televised and sustained by an industry every bit as hungry as the celebrity press.

The real distinction is not restraint. It is permission.

Royal families are assumed to belong amid palaces, couture and priceless heirlooms. Working-class celebrities are expected to remain relatable even after becoming rich. Spend too little and they are stingy; spend too much and they are “common.” Their money may be new, the implication goes, but the rules guarding glamour are very old.

Rooney and McLoughlin’s wedding may have been over the top. That was part of its charm. It was loud, aspirational and gloriously unconcerned with patrician understatement: a fairy tale with football wages rather than inherited titles.

And perhaps that is what truly irritated the taste police. The couple did not wait to be invited into the castle. They booked Italy, brought their own entourage and built one themselves.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a sympathetic commentary portraying Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin’s relationship as a modern fairy tale and defending their decision to sell their wedding pictures to OK magazine?
counterfactuals.output:
### Wayne and Coleen: A Fairy Tale for the Magazine Age

Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin’s story has many of the ingredients of a traditional fairy tale: childhood sweethearts, extraordinary success and a lavish wedding watched with fascination far beyond their Liverpool roots. Yet what makes their romance compelling is not that it resembles an old-fashioned fantasy, but that it reflects the world in which they actually live—a world of football fame, tabloid attention and relentless public scrutiny.

Their decision to sell their wedding photographs to *OK!* magazine has inevitably attracted criticism. Some will say that a private declaration of love should not become a commercial transaction. But privacy for a couple as famous as Wayne and Coleen is not easily preserved simply by refusing a magazine deal. Interest in their wedding was guaranteed. Photographers would have pursued unofficial pictures, guests might have been offered money for snapshots, and newspapers would have filled pages with speculation.

By agreeing to an exclusive, the couple could regain some control. They could decide which images entered the public domain, present the celebration as they wished it to be seen and protect their guests from an even more intrusive media chase. If newspapers and magazines were certain to profit from public curiosity, it is hardly unreasonable for Wayne and Coleen to benefit too.

Nor does accepting payment make their feelings less genuine. Modern celebrity weddings exist in an uncomfortable space between private emotion and public spectacle. A commercial arrangement may surround the ceremony, but it does not define the marriage. Love is not invalidated by glossy photographs any more than it is validated by secrecy.

Their fairy tale is therefore a distinctly modern one—not a story of anonymous princes and secluded castles, but of two young people who grew up together and then found themselves living under an unforgiving spotlight. Selling the photographs was not necessarily a rejection of romance. It was a pragmatic response to fame: an attempt to manage the public appetite while keeping at least part of their day on their own terms.

The true test of their relationship will never be the magazine cover or the size of the fee. It will be the life they build after the cameras have gone.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

Yet the pressure has helped turn her into a celebrity in her own right. She has built a career through magazine columns, television appearances, fashion endorsements and style projects—no longer simply known as a footballer’s fiancée.

Their story began long before fame and fortune. The pair met as children in the Liverpool suburb of Croxteth and began dating as teenagers, before Wayne became one of England’s best-known footballers. That shared history is central to their public image: a childhood romance surviving sudden wealth, sporting fame and repeated scandal.

And amid the conspicuous luxury, the couple have sought to add a charitable note. Rather than simply receiving extravagant presents, they have reportedly encouraged guests to make donations benefiting children’s causes, including charities and hospitals in their home region.

For supporters, it is a modern fairy tale. For critics, it is an expertly marketed celebrity spectacle. Either way, Britain will be watching.
